newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Ahold Q1 sales jump, sees full-year profit growth.
newsitem.headline: Ahold Q1 sales jump, sees full-year profit growth.

text.p: Dutch supermarket group Ahold saw sales grow 48.2 percent in the first quarter of 1997 and the company said on Tuesday it expected considerable profit growth over the full year.

Ahold issued a sales report ahead of its shareholders' meeting showing first-quarter consolidated group sales rose to 14.0 billion guilders ($7.2 billion) and predicting improved turnover translating to higher net and per-share earnings for the year.
"This boils down to an increase of 30 to 45 percent in net profits and a 12 to 20 percent growth in earnings per share," chairman Cees van der Hoeven told reporters at a news conference.
He added the expected profit rise was not including positive effects of currency rates, which were considerable at the moment, having had a positive effect of 9.8 percent on first quarter sales.
In the U.S., first quarter sales showed a year-on-year growth of 53.9 percent to $4.2 billion, Ahold said.
Excluding the effect of the $3.0 billion Stop & Shop acquisition in July last year, overall first quarter sales grew by 17.1 percent.
Ahold was continuing to look for acquisitions on the U.S. East Coast, chairman Cees van der Hoeven told reporters.
"We are looking at sales of one billion dollars plus... It's quality operators that we're looking for."

Board member Rob Zwartendijk predicted a wave of mergers and acquisitions in the U.S. supermarket business, noting in Europe the five biggest retailers had some 80 percent of the market, while the top five in the U.S. had only about 20 percent.
"There's a lot more consolidation to come and we will play a part in it," Zwartendijk said.
Turnover in the Asia Pacific region mushroomed to 274 million guilders in the first quarter, from just 56 million in the full year of 1996, and would continue to boom, Ahold said.
"At the end of this year, we will have between 150 and 200 shops in Asia...We think we will outstrip the one billion guilder turnover mark this year," spokesman Hans Gobes said.
Colleague Jan Hol said activities in the region, which generated a 20.6 million guilder loss in 1996, would remain a loss-making until the turn of the century.
"We expect to break even by 1999 or 2000," he said.

Hol said Ahold was currently exploring further opportunities to expand in the Shanghai region, with its 17 million inhabitants, where Ahold is already active through its joint venture with a unit of China Venturetech Investment Corp (CVIC).
"I'm not sure we will finalise anything this year...But it does look good at the moment," he said.
Van der Hoeven repeated an earlier statement that Ahold would issue shares in order to finance major acquisitions.
"Anything costing more than 500 million guilders...will be, at least partially, financed through the issue of shares, but only if it immediately contributes to growth in earnings per share," he said.

Ahold's first quarter sales in the Netherlands grew by 6.1 percent to 4.7 billion guilders and turnover in the rest of Europe went up by 32.1 percent to 693 million guilders. Sales in Brazil totalled 474 million guilders.
Last year, Ahold posted a net profit of 632.4 million guilders, or 4.30 guilders per share.
The company reports first quarter profits on June 12.
Ahold's shares closed up 2.00 guilders at 142.00 guilders on the Amsterdam Stock Exchange.
